name: Freya Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We farm Hillhead, 250 hectares, with a herd of 110 suckler cows and malting barley that goes to the distillery down the valley. I'm usually feeding by half six, then it's whatever the day brings: a calf with scour, a broken water trough, a field to roll. Ross, my husband, is a mechanic at the machinery dealer in town, so he fixes our kit at weekends whether he likes it or not. We've two youngsters, Isla and Jamie, and I take on an apprentice from the agricultural college every year.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Because somebody took me on, once. You don't learn farming from a book, you learn it from someone shouting at you across a muddy field and then buying you a pie after. I use the odd AI tool to sort out forms, but I'm not one for chasing every new thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that, back to work. Probably at church on Sunday, someone would ask. I'd say the tools are handy for forms and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine with it. I've got used to asking the chat thing about forms, and I'd keep that. The farm doesn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going the same. Keep the apprentice scheme going, sell the calves, sell the barley. I might put money into a new handling system for the cattle, which I've wanted for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a new handling system mean, for someone who doesn't farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the gates and pens and crush, the cage that holds a cow still, so you can treat cattle safely. Ours is older than me. I've been kicked in that crush more times than I've been to the dentist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the apprentices be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in this picture. They'd still learn the same things I did, with maybe a phone app or two. That's how it should be.

S0.say: I'd say at church on Sunday that that's that and it's back to work. The tools are handy for forms and not much else.
S0.think: Privately I'd be fine with it and would keep using the chat tool for forms. The farm itself wouldn't change.
S0.do: Keeps going as before, with the yearly apprentice and the calf and barley sales. Invests in a new cattle handling system she's wanted for years.
S0.quote: I've been kicked in that crush more times than I've been to the dentist.
S0.fieldNote: Freya's pride is in passing skills on through her yearly apprentice, which she ties to someone once taking her on. She uses AI only for forms. Her concrete wish in this picture is a safer cattle handling system, not anything digital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers have always adapted and we'll do it again. I'd say the colleges should teach the new kit alongside the old skills. I'd say it at the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. My worry is the apprentices, because if the robots take the simple jobs, what do the youngsters learn on? You can't start at the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a season to see what the big farms bought, then buy one bit of kit that's proven, probably a robot feeder for the cattle shed. I'd get Ross to learn how to fix it, since that's his trade. And I'd keep the apprentice scheme, but add the robot work to what they learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little worry about the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can't start at the top. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I started mucking out, then feeding, then calving. Each job taught me the next one. If a robot does all the mucking out, the next generation will be managing cows they've never had to clean up after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ross's job change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His trade would grow, I think. More machines, more breakdowns. He'd be busier, and he'd moan about it, and he'd be secretly pleased.

S1.say: I'd say farmers have always adapted and will again, and that colleges should teach new kit alongside old skills. I'd say it at the young farmers' club.
S1.think: Privately I'd be fine, but I worry about apprentices, because if robots take the simple jobs the young ones have nothing to learn on. You can't start at the top.
S1.do: Waits a season to see what larger farms buy, then purchases one proven machine, probably a robot feeder for the cattle shed. Has Ross learn to repair it and adds robot work to what the apprentices learn.
S1.feel: Calm, with a small worry about the young ones.
S1.quote: If a robot does all the mucking out, the next generation will be managing cows they've never had to clean up after.
S1.fieldNote: Freya's distinctive worry is about the ladder of learning: if robots take the bottom rungs, apprentices can't climb. She waits a season and then buys proven kit. She expects her husband's mechanic trade to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will have to pull together, because the government won't be ready. I'd say people should keep working at whatever they can and not wait for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me a lot. We own most of the land, so we'd survive. But the distillery could grow its own barley with robots, and the beef price would drop if big robot farms flooded the market. Two years doesn't give me time to wait and watch, which is how I like to do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the handling system and keep the cash. I'd cut back at home, the holiday, the new car. I'd talk to the distillery about a longer contract, for local barley, sold as local. I'd lean on Ross's job, which might hold up longer, and on my parents if we needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but not sleeping well either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still take on an apprentice that year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard one. I'd want to, but I'd be lying if I said there was a future in it for them. I'd feel like I was teaching a lad to shoe horses the year the tractor came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Isla and Jamie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we've got the farm and each other, and that's more than most. Isla's twelve and she'd ask straight questions. I'd answer them as straight as I could.

S2.say: I'd say families and communities will have to pull together because the government won't be ready. I'd say people should keep working at whatever they can rather than wait for handouts.
S2.think: Privately it worries me a lot: we'd survive because we own most of the land, but the distillery could grow its own barley and beef prices would fall. Two years gives no time to wait and watch, which is how I like to work.
S2.do: Halts the handling system and keeps the cash, and cuts household spending like the holiday and a new car. Asks the distillery for a longer contract for barley sold as local, and leans on Ross's job and her parents if needed.
S2.feel: Anxious, not panicking but sleeping badly.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I was teaching a lad to shoe horses the year the tractor came.
S2.fieldNote: Freya's land gives her a floor, but her wait-and-watch habit is useless in two years. Her answer leans on family and on selling barley as local. She struggles over whether taking on an apprentice would be fair, which goes to the heart of her values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a family farm to get ready, if it starts now. I'd say apprenticeships need to change, not stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me my season of watching. I'd see the first robot farms, I'd see what breaks, and I'd move in year two or three. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more in the first year, for planning and records, to get used to them. In year two or three I'd buy a robot feeder and a self-driving tractor for the barley, second-hand if I could. And I'd change the apprentice scheme so the youngsters learn to run and fix the robots too, with Ross teaching that bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of the farm you'd keep without robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calving. I'd keep that by hand as long as I live. Some things you do with your hands because they matter, not because nobody's built a machine for them yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the distillery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the distillery to sell the local story: barley from Hillhead, grown by a family. That's worth something, in five years or fifty.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for a family farm to get ready if it starts now. I'd say apprenticeships need to change, not stop.
S3.think: Privately five years gives me my season of watching: I'd see the first robot farms and what breaks, then move in year two or three. I'd be fine.
S3.do: Uses AI tools more in the first year for planning and records, then buys a robot feeder and a self-driving tractor for the barley, second-hand if possible, in year two or three. Changes the apprentice scheme so trainees learn to run and fix robots, with Ross teaching.
S3.quote: Some things you do with your hands because they matter, not because nobody's built a machine for them yet.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Freya keep her usual rhythm of watching first, and that restores her confidence. She'd adapt the apprentice scheme rather than end it, using her husband's skills. Keeping calving by hand is a line she draws on values, not economics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and there's no excuse for not getting ready. I'd say the young ones need proper apprenticeships in the new work, not just college courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine, and so would the farm. I'd be 53 and probably handing more over to whoever comes next. What worries me is whether Isla or Jamie would want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd farm on for a few years and keep the apprentice scheme going. Around year four or five I'd start bringing in robots, a piece at a time. I'd put money aside so Isla and Jamie could study whatever they wanted, and I'd tell them the farm is theirs if they want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if neither of them wanted the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd find an apprentice who did. I've had some good ones. Farms don't have to pass to blood, they have to pass to someone who'll get up at six for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything at church or in the community?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the church hall used for something, maybe evening classes. People will need somewhere to meet, if they're not meeting at work.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning and there's no excuse not to be ready. Young people need proper apprenticeships in the new work, not just college courses.
S4.think: Privately I'd be fine and so would the farm, at 53 and starting to hand more over. My worry is whether Isla or Jamie will want it.
S4.do: Farms on and keeps the apprentice scheme for a few years, then brings in robots piece by piece around year four or five. Saves so Isla and Jamie can study what they choose, and tells them the farm is theirs if they want it.
S4.quote: Farms don't have to pass to blood, they have to pass to someone who'll get up at six for them.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Freya's question is succession, not survival. She surprises herself by saying the farm need not pass to family, only to someone committed. She also thinks about the church hall as a meeting place, showing her community focus.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I couldn't watch first, and I always watch first. What would help is apprenticeships in the new kit, paid for properly, so young people can still learn a trade by doing it. And a long contract with the distillery for local barley.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it does to towns. If nobody works on the farms, the pub shuts, the shop shuts, the school shrinks. That's what I'd worry about after the farm.

headlineQuote: You don't learn farming from a book, you learn it from someone shouting at you across a muddy field and then buying you a pie after.
portrait: Freya Young is 43 and farms Hillhead, a 250-hectare beef and malting barley farm, with her husband Ross, a machinery mechanic, helping at weekends. She takes on an apprentice every year because someone once took her on, and she uses AI tools only now and then for forms. Traditional and family-minded, she prefers communities pulling together over government help and likes to watch a season before buying anything. She's calm in the slower scenarios, anxious with AGI in two years because she can't wait and watch, and with ten years her thoughts turn to who will take the farm on.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because she couldn't watch others first before acting, which is how she always works.
whatWouldHelp: Properly funded apprenticeships in the new machines, and a long contract with the distillery for local barley.
